sections.heading: Eight current advocacy priorities
sections.intro: These priorities organize current advocacy without replacing SBWPC’s complete adopted policy positions. Open one issue at a time: review SBWPC’s position, the public bodies with decision-making authority and one clear action for each current advocacy priority.

items.title: Elections, Voting Rights and Democratic Participation
items.summary: Protect access to the ballot, reliable election administration, fair representation and meaningful political participation.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC supports broad, equitable voting access, accurate election information, accountable administration and public participation free from intimidation or discrimination.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
County election officials, California election authorities, legislators, courts and Congress—depending on the action.
One Clear Action
Use official voter information, support election protection and ask public officials to preserve equal access and transparent administration.

items.title: Immigration, Due Process and Civil Liberties
items.summary: Advance humane immigration policy, family unity, legal protection and community trust.

children.text: SBWPC Position

SBWPC supports comprehensive and compassionate reform, a path to citizenship, asylum protections, DACA and equal protection under law while opposing harassment, family separation and unlawful or inhumane detention.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Congress, federal agencies, courts, California officials, local governments and law-enforcement policy bodies.
One Clear Action
Ask the relevant official to protect due process, family unity, legal access and transparent limits on enforcement collaboration.

items.title: Equal Rights Amendment and Constitutional Equality
items.summary: Make equality regardless of sex an explicit and durable constitutional principle.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC supports recognition and enforcement of the Equal Rights Amendment and stronger legal protection against sex discrimination.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Congress, federal executive institutions, courts and state officials involved in constitutional processes.
One Clear Action
Ask federal officials to state their ERA position and identify the concrete action they will take to advance constitutional equality.

items.title: Reproductive Justice and Equitable Healthcare
items.summary: Protect bodily autonomy and ensure comprehensive, affordable and nondiscriminatory healthcare throughout the life cycle.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC supports reproductive self-determination, universal access to quality healthcare, control over personal medical decisions and the elimination of discrimination in health policy and practice.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Congress, federal and state health agencies, California officials, insurers, healthcare systems and local public-health bodies.
One Clear Action
Ask the responsible public body to protect access, privacy, affordability and equitable treatment while removing discriminatory barriers.

items.title: Childcare, Paid Leave and Women’s Economic Security
items.summary: Treat care as economic infrastructure and remove structural barriers to women’s employment, advancement and financial security.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC supports affordable, high-quality childcare and early education, fair compensation for care workers, pay equity, paid family leave and policies that strengthen family economic stability.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Congress, California legislators and agencies, local governments, employers and public funding bodies.
One Clear Action
Ask for sustained public investment, fair compensation and measurable access goals for families and care workers.

items.title: Climate Action, Coastal Protection and Environmental Justice
items.summary: Protect public health, communities and natural resources through accountable climate and environmental policy.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC supports a healthy and just environment, climate action, pollution prevention and meaningful community participation in decisions affecting land, water, air and public health.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Federal and California environmental agencies, legislators, local land-use bodies, courts and public boards.
One Clear Action
Ask for transparent review, public-health safeguards, enforceable mitigation and meaningful participation before consequential decisions.

items.title: Freedom from Gender-Based Violence and Gun Violence
items.summary: Advance prevention, survivor-centered services, accountable institutions and community safety.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC opposes interpersonal and sexual violence, trafficking, harassment, exploitation and gun violence while supporting prevention, culturally competent services and responsive justice systems.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Congress, California legislators, courts, law enforcement, public-health agencies, schools, employers and local governments.
One Clear Action
Ask for survivor-centered policy, prevention funding, accountable enforcement and evidence-based public-safety measures.

items.title: Feminist Leadership and Representative Public Power
items.summary: Build a government that reflects community diversity and expands women’s access, voice and power.

children.text: SBWPC Position
SBWPC supports women and feminist leaders seeking elected and appointed office and works to remove institutional barriers to equal representation and opportunity.
Who Has Decision-Making Power
Voters, appointing authorities, elected bodies, political organizations, public boards and candidate-development institutions.
One Clear Action
Recruit a candidate, apply for an appointed role, support leadership training or join SBWPC’s candidate and appointments work.

hero.heading: Equality Must Be Explicit and Durable
hero.body: The Equal Rights Amendment is a century-long effort to place equality of rights regardless of sex explicitly in the United States Constitution. SBWPC supports the ERA as part of its adopted feminist public-policy framework.

stats.label: Current Status
stats.note: Thirty-eight states have voted to ratify the ERA

image.alt: Santa Barbara Women's Political Committee ERA Equal Rights Amendment badge: Equality, Justice, Opportunity

sections.heading: The numerical threshold has been reached but certification remains disputed

children.text: Thirty-eight states.
Virginia’s 2020 action brought the number of states that voted to ratify the ERA to thirty-eight.
National Archives position.
NARA states that the ERA cannot currently be certified as part of the Constitution because of the ratification deadline and established legal, judicial and procedural decisions.
Current congressional pathway.
H.J. Res. 80 and S.J. Res. 38 in the 119th Congress seek to establish the ERA as valid notwithstanding the original time limit.
The ERA’s legal status remains contested. This page distinguishes the thirty-eight-state ratification count from the separate question of certification and publication as part of the Constitution.

sections.heading: Constitutional equality remains unfinished
sections.intro: SBWPC supports ratification of the ERA and CEDAW. The organization’s adopted position papers explicitly call for constitutional equality and ratification of both the Equal Rights Amendment and CEDAW.

children.text: Equal Rights (ERA & CEDAW)

Women are not explicitly accorded equal rights and protections in the United States Constitution. The United States is the only developed nation that has not ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1979.
We demand the ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment and of CEDAW by the United States.

items.title: First Introduced
items.body: The Equal Rights Amendment is first introduced in Congress.

items.title: Congressional Passage
items.body: Congress approves the ERA and sends it to the states with an initial seven-year ratification deadline.
Congress extends the ratification deadline to June 30, 1982.
The extended deadline passes with thirty-five states having ratified by that date.
Nevada votes to ratify the ERA.
Illinois votes to ratify the ERA.

items.title: Thirty-Eighth State
items.body: Virginia votes to ratify, bringing the total number of state ratification actions to thirty-eight.
The National Archives states that it cannot certify and publish the ERA under existing legal and procedural decisions.
H.J. Res. 80 and S.J. Res. 38 are introduced in the 119th Congress to establish ratification notwithstanding the time limit.

items.label: Today
items.title: Current Debate
items.body: The legal effect of the deadline, certification and congressional action remains the central dispute.

sections.heading: Explicit constitutional equality has broad implications
sections.intro: Supporters of the ERA argue that an explicit constitutional guarantee would strengthen the legal foundation for addressing sex-based discrimination across public life. These are the six areas of public life in which ERA supporters argue an explicit constitutional equality guarantee could strengthen the legal framework against sex-based discrimination.

cards.title: Pay & Employment
cards.body: Equal treatment in pay, employment opportunity and workplace protections.

cards.title: Education
cards.body: Equal access, opportunity and treatment in educational institutions and programs.

cards.title: Gender-Based Violence
cards.body: A constitutional equality lens for laws and government responses involving sex-based violence and discrimination.

cards.title: Bodily Autonomy
cards.body: Constitutional arguments concerning sex equality, bodily autonomy and government treatment.

cards.title: Public Institutions
cards.body: Equal treatment in government programs, public systems and civic participation.

cards.title: Equal Protection
cards.body: An explicit textual guarantee that equality of rights may not be denied or abridged on account of sex.

sections.heading: Understand the protections available to voters

cards.title: Vote free from threats or interference
cards.body: Federal and state law protect voters from intimidation, threats, coercion and interference. Federal law prohibits intimidation, threats and coercion throughout the voting process, including registration, voting and ballot counting. If a problem is happening, contact the election official or supervisor at the voting location and call or text 866-OUR-VOTE for nonpartisan assistance.

cards.title: Accessible and private voting
cards.body: California provides accessible polling places, accessible voting equipment and Remote Accessible Vote-by-Mail. California requires polling places and vote centers to be accessible and to provide accessible voting equipment. RAVBM allows eligible voters to access and mark ballot selections using compatible technology, then print and return the ballot selections by mail or in person.

cards.title: Voting information in multiple languages
cards.body: California provides official voting assistance in ten languages (English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai and Vietnamese), while Election Protection offers additional multilingual nonpartisan hotlines for English, Spanish, Asian-language and Arabic voter assistance.
